cleaned_transcript:
Host: Chris, AI is making software so easy to build. So why can't every team just build their own internal software tools?

Chris Guthrie: I mean, this is a question I think we've both gotten very recently, and the honest answer is: you can. It's a thing you can do. But the difference between wisdom and knowledge is knowing whether you should do the thing you can. I'd point to the rest of the business landscape — the U.S. cannabis industry did $30.5 billion in 2025. What other industries out there are vibe coding their supply chain, their AR/AP, their customer documentation, their sales processes? Where else is it happening? Not to say you can't build useful tools that hone in on a specific piece of your data, but where's the aerospace company vibe coding their supply chain? Where's the cosmetics company vibe coding their CRM? There was that whole doom-and-gloom LinkedIn cycle about "SaaS is dead, SaaS is dead," and more and more people are discovering there's a lot more chip than salsa right now. I think we're going to keep seeing that. So the answer to the question is: show me another industry that's doing it successfully. Or do cannabis entrepreneurs just have that latent need to walk all the way out on the limb and say, with two middle fingers up, "look what I'm doing"? Should you do it?

Host: Do we think the idea is more about — hey, my business is really lean and tight and I see this as a cost-saving move? Is that the origin of the idea, or is it something else?

Chris Guthrie: I think there's some cost saving in it, sure. But I also think there's a pathological need to be first — to be doing something nobody else is doing. Everybody's in the cannabis industry now. You're not automatically the top dog anymore just by saying "I'm in cannabis." For a while people would hesitate to even say it, because everyone would suddenly be so interested. Now it's more like, "cool, I do insurance." I don't really know, man. I don't really know.

Host: Because I think vibe coding tools have their place. Where I start to struggle is with businesses that are vertical or semi-vertical — cultivation, manufacturing, some retail, trying to stay compliant, trying to keep everything moving in the right direction. And hearing some of these teams say they're just going to build these tools internally feels like another weight on their shoulders — another responsibility to figure out. It's almost a distraction: we know cultivation is solid, we know extraction is close, we could probably do better on supply chain, but instead I'm going to spend my finite time and resources over here. I wonder if that's a way of convincing the brain that this is a better approach because there are cost-saving metrics attached to it. But I think that's part of the problem.

Chris Guthrie: Sure — if it works, it could be a cost saving. If it works.

Host: Maybe define "if it works," so we're all on the same page. Because I think that's the real difference — you can vibe-code an app live right now that runs. But what does "works" actually mean?

Chris Guthrie: Okay. "Works" means getting data into your system about your inventory — how that inventory is being used, when it needs to be used or consumed, where it's going to be used and consumed, and by whom, at what rate. I'm building the world's ugliest outline here on my thumb, but at bare minimum you need to be able to record that data. Then, once it's recorded, it needs to be organized and laid out in tables in a way that's readable to the next person in the process flow — the next person in the supply chain, whatever team you're working with — because you're not going to be in the same room as them anymore. That's part of why people think they can do this themselves: they remember running a hundred lights and crushing it. You're not running a hundred lights anymore. You're running a thousand lights across ten different rooms in two different buildings. So bare minimum: can you record the information? Once it's recorded, how is it organized so other people can access it? And then does that information flow to different departments? Does wet flower harvest translate into a drying-room production scheme or drying-room activities? Do those activities then yield a new raw material input for manufacturing?

Chris Guthrie: It's very easy — and this isn't specific to cannabis, I work in ERP for other industries too — for any business to think it's simpler than it actually is, because it all lives in the founder's head. They've been doing it for thirty years, they can just do it. But when you actually unpack the complexity of manufacturing — never mind cultivating a raw material for heavily regulated processing and manufacturing all the way to CPG — it's much more complicated than people realize. And there's real risk in that: all the process living in your head. I tell prospects and customers I have a good relationship with, somewhat like a smart-ass: what happens if you get hit by a bus? What happens? My business mentor told me — if you're running a business that can't operate while you take a month-long sabbatical, you're not running a business, you have a hobby. My cousin used to run rally cars; you can have expensive hobbies, but that's not a business. So that's my answer to your question.

Host: I think what you said about it all living in your head is so easy to relate to, and I think that's part of the path a lot of teams are on. There are teams out there thinking, "we could just vibe code this, Johnny's really smart, we'll hire an AI consultant," and then, "okay, does it live in the cloud or on a desktop? How do we sync information? How do we handle unit transfers?" When someone orders 10 versus 25, and they're using different units, all of that has to carry through correctly. If you're doing calculations or adjustments, most teams run things a little differently out of the box, and you have to account for that. And my favorite part of software: when you edit one field, it sometimes has corresponding effects on other fields down the road that you didn't realize up front. And AI, as powerful as it is, can't infer that you're changing something on your cultivation page but should also be thinking about the effect on finished goods down the line at a given rate. It doesn't know that. So you set yourself up for a disaster path where it's easy to get started but really hard to go from "is this working as an MVP" to something functional you can actually deploy as a company.

Chris Guthrie: Most of the cannabis operators I work with lovingly call their own employees idiots. So — is what you vibe-coded on a Saturday and Sunday going to withstand the full-contact violence of your production and cultivation team? They're busy, they're sticky. What kind of UI did you actually build for them? Are there any stopgaps to keep them from missing data points? And going back to the vibe coding idea — unless you have a Git repository and a real development environment in front of you, Claude is doing all that code and you don't know what's going on back there. Worst case, you have something that works for you and a couple of associates for a couple of months. Then, as you're getting ready for production, you discover there's some crucial field that doesn't map, some workflow that doesn't tie together, something's broken — and you can't find it, because that was a vibe-code session from a month and a half ago, and who knows if that decision tree is even still in the model. You will not find that mistake. You can review and normalize the code all you want, but this gets back to what's actually wrong with cannabis technology specifically: tech debt. You will incur tech debt vibe coding. Anybody who's spent a weekend trying to build an app knows you get to something that's almost good, and then at the last minute it breaks, and fixing that becomes a cascade of failure — because vibe coding makes you feel awesome, and ChatGPT and Claude are there to stroke your ego. But unless you actually understand what's happening at a computer science level, you're building a house of cards every single time. It will not stand any sort of violence.

Host: It does feel so good, and I think that's part of the problem — it's almost addictive, like a video game. You have a problem, you get started so quickly, and Claude shows you a working prototype so fast that you think, "my God, that took fifteen minutes, I'm going to solve my whole problem in ten hours, I'm going to have an enterprise-grade tool, I'll roll it out, go back to my day job, and be a hero." That's part of the challenge, and as the industry evolves I think teams forget there are businesses that have spent enormous amounts of time and money, for better or worse, learning how to set up the correct infrastructure — data protection policy, privacy policy, computer infrastructure policy — working through the surprising edge cases, so their teams can focus on what they do best: selling the molecule, which is THC.

Chris Guthrie: Right. From a software ecosystem point of view, software is about setting something up, running it, seeing what happens, and correcting for mistakes. The cannabis software industry has been pushing those dominoes down for twelve years, tops. I work with a Microsoft platform called Business Central that we've customized for the cannabis industry — we're all from the industry ourselves. We have the benefit of literally tens of millions of hours of use cases, business scenarios, and breaks: brand-new business processes people want, accrual models, item structures, master data numerical sequences. You're not going to ask Business Central to do anything it hasn't been asked to do before. Without naming names, you will, on the daily, ask cannabis software to accommodate an item structure, a BOM configuration, multi-output finished goods from multi-input production schemes — and if the vendor hasn't seen it before, the software only knows what it knows. The developers can only solve what they've had to solve. If they haven't seen it, it won't solve it. That's why cannabis operators keep running into these walls of "yeah, it's coming in Q3," "yeah, it's coming in Q4" — never mind all the changes that some random Metrc update forces people to accommodate. You can only solve for the problems you've actually encountered with software.

Host: And just to be clear — Microsoft, as in the Microsoft.

Chris Guthrie: The Microsoft. The Seattle-based, Bill Gates-founded Microsoft.

Host: Because sometimes I feel like we have to give some of these companies their flowers. They've been around a long time, they've established infrastructure and brand credibility you can lean on, and that has to come with something — because setting up these software environments, you've seen it, I've seen it. There's the foundational level, there's an idea, and then taking that idea to fruition requires passing through a bunch of steps and environments to make sure you're not just shipping and hoping it works — crossing your fingers — because it has to go through a testing phase to make sure things don't break, don't hurt other things, don't reset your entire module. Because the last thing your team wants, on a day it has no resources to spare, is to add a step where clicking a button doesn't work, and it's "hey Chris, I'm going to need two weeks to get back to you because I have no idea why it's not working."

Chris Guthrie: Yeah — or, "hey, Elliot's on PTO, he just left for his wedding, he's the one who knows the code, I can't fix the spreadsheet ERP, I don't know what we're going to do." That's also an infrastructure problem, and it goes back to code integrity and whether you can really vibe code or not. Microsoft spends most of its time maintaining the stability, repeatability, and deployability of its code. Business Central is now a standard set of fields and APIs that doesn't change — you don't customize your ERP core anymore, that's been an industry-wide shift in the ERP space. The core compute and structure is hardened and set, and you choose how to interact with it. That's what makes Business Central and 365 Cannabis powerful for this industry: it's built for cultivation and manufacturing, but malleable enough to accept nuance and different process flows — because every grower I've ever met was sure they were the only person to ever grow cannabis successfully or the "right" way. Let's be real. We can accommodate all of that, because there's a solid infrastructure backed by Microsoft — love or hate big tech, but they've got a battleship, and you can build a house on it and they'll sail you around.

Host: Do you think people sometimes misrepresent the cost involved? I think getting started now is deceptively easy because the cloud makes it feel so accessible. But once you start using those APIs and racking up bills when things don't work correctly, you start realizing your $10,000 budget isn't going to be sufficient. Plus people forget hosting costs are genuinely expensive. That's the moment it hits: you've got a great product, but you want multiple people using it across different sites, so it has to be hosted in the cloud — and Microsoft or Amazon will happily host it for you, but it's going to cost fifteen hundred dollars a month, and you're like, "for what?"

Chris Guthrie: "You want to put your stuff in this box over here? Yeah, that's what it costs."

Host: And that's where people think, "I'm going to save three thousand dollars a month." Maybe. Or you spend four thousand dollars a month and end up with a non-working product that drives two teammates crazy, and you're left wondering, "what did we even do, it'd be great to have that fifty thousand dollars back."

Chris Guthrie: Or you could have invested that fifty thousand dollars in a system that comes with hosting and is stable. If something seems free, you're the product — that's exactly the promise of it. You'll make huge steps in the first fifteen minutes, but every hour after that, you move the needle a little less. God forbid you build something into your vibe-coded ERP that requires AI tokens, because now it's not just that you spent a bunch of tokens vibe coding it — it's going to keep consuming tokens every single time someone runs a query, a rendering, or a relational ask. What's that going to do to your costs?

Host: That part is exactly where people want to go — they've got all this data and they want predictive insights from it. But that's where vibe coding your own ERP or your own tools leads to more problems, because if the AI doesn't have clean, accurate, directional access to all your data, you're just handing it a mess and saying, "here, help me understand this."

Chris Guthrie: Let me paint you the picture: Claude will say, "wow, this is a great data set, you've really collected a lot of insightful information, great job — but I can't do anything with this. This is a pepperoni pizza, correct?" And it's like, no, Claude, you're drunk, go home. But that's a coin slot opening up on your laptop: please deposit seventy-five thousand dollars. What you said about people wanting predictive insight is more and more what I'm hearing from organizations: "we've been going along for a while, but I need to look into the future a little. I need to be ready." Everybody's survived up to this point on sheer determination. What ERP is supposed to do is use your data to let you make predictive decisions — know what raw materials you'll need and when, who needs to be at work based on labor demand, predict that based on current production you'll have this inventory at this time and it'll cost about that much. That's the actual information you need. So — are you a computer scientist? Great, you told Claude your business flow and it said you need this, this, and this. But can you take that descriptive data and turn it into a predictive set of tables that says: if this number, then this number, then this number — that's a yield projection. If this input on this schedule equals this times this, that's a predictive tool. The cannabis industry is built on a descriptive data-capture structure. Every seed-to-sale system out there started life as a Metrc skin or a BioTrack skin, one way or another. People tried connecting with Leaf Data, and that was just a brick wall.

Chris Guthrie: People need ERP for predictive insight, but I don't think the data sitting in cannabis tools today even supports that, because it's just a record of what already happened. You'll still have to ask the AI to extrapolate what's going to happen — and that work has already been done by others. So again: are you pathologically conditioned by being in the cannabis industry to have to do everything yourself and be first with a brand-new idea? Or are you willing to accept that humanity has already done this work for you? You don't have to reinvent the wheel — ERP is the wheels of business at this point.

Host: Kind of blending the two — having a foundational ERP you can trust, plus a data schema that lets you pull the right variables. With that foundation, you can get real predictive insight. Without it, you're essentially saying "this guess times this guess plus this Claude guess gives me this guess," and I don't think that's what people actually want. Which brings me back to: is this the best use of your team's time? Capital is so scarce — are we spending it figuring out what we do better than anyone else, or are we distracting ourselves from our core focus? Are we a cultivation company, a retail company, an extraction company? What do we do better than anyone else, and how do we deploy money as a tool to get there?

Chris Guthrie: If a cannabis company asks itself what it does better than anybody else, and the answer is "vibe coding," you should turn off your lights — that's not what your team does best.

Host: I think what happens is people convince themselves: we could save cost, we've got two really smart employees, maybe we hire an "AI consultant" — which is a very popular term I keep hearing — and I have no idea how that's going to turn out, except that it might just be setting money on fire, and in six months you realize that was a massive waste of time, energy, and money. It's so much harder to actually pull off. Maybe start with the goal in mind: what are we trying to achieve? Because if it's saving money, it's probably not going to save you money in the long run.

Chris Guthrie: Right — you made huge strides Saturday and Sunday on your tool, but the quality of the code and the flow you produce shrinks with every iteration after that. There's no way you keep up with that diminishing return while building an AI tool. What even is an "AI consultant" as a job? Something I heard in Chicago from Chris Violas of Blaze on a panel we were both on, and something I really admire Blaze for doing: they've got very strong data governance rules. All their base information and instructions are stored in a vault, in a repository — because they learned, apparently pretty early on, that Claude and GPT drift. In the middle of a vibe coding session, the model will actually stop referencing the original data set you gave it and start incorporating something else you never asked for. So first and foremost: do you know how to use AI? Do you know if a problem is even solvable by AI? I hope people do — people think they do, and that's why they get the idea they can build a vibe-coded ERP or CRM. But I guarantee that, just like cannabis operators get defensive when a non-cannabis person says "I'm going to start a cannabis company" — somebody who's never touched the industry telling someone who was a backpack boy in 2009, "yeah, you're gonna grow, sure" — computer scientists and ERP practitioners feel the same insult when someone says "I'm going to build an ERP over the weekend with Claude." You don't know what you don't know. Those are the holes you're going to fall into.

Host: I don't want to sh on AI building — it's a fond project of mine too, for a long time. But it has to fit into the chain, and from the conversations I've been hearing recently, people are misallocating how that thought process works. What's the goal in mind? If it's to save money, you're probably not going to save money. If it's to improve a specific piece of your data structure to make better predictive decisions, then AI can absolutely help. Setting up that foundation means understanding how the tools actually work, and having a realistic view of what they can and can't do. That's the part I think is most important.

Chris Guthrie: It is, because AI is not creative. If you ask AI to create something, it has literally the whole internet to pull from — the collected knowledge of humanity. Are you sure it's going to pull the right context, the right data, the right history? That's what Chris Violas is doing with his data repository at Blaze: every single query is pointed at Blaze's own data. So do you know how to corral your queries first? Are you sure you're asking the AI a question it can actually solve? Because if you ask it to invent a data structure for you, what is that even going to be? Are you willing to rest your five-million-dollar business — say you're a small operator — on a piece of software that's a month old? That's bananas to me.

Host: I start thinking about the industry maturing and the big players coming in wanting to find the right partner or gain access to the market. They start evaluating a target's tech stack: "show me the tools your team uses." And if the answer is "we built our own CRM, we vibe-coded this dashboard," they're going to think, if this is the foundation, I'm petrified to see what the books look like — because it shows something about the decision-making. Businesses want to see certain things to check the box on being the right partner. That's the piece you alluded to earlier: the industry was so entrepreneurial and "we have to do this ourselves," but there are elements where you have to lean on the tools and partners that are already established.

Chris Guthrie: The only thing you needed in early cannabis to make millions of dollars was the balls to do it. You still need balls, but now you also need caution and patience. You have to grow these businesses the way you grow a plant — you can't put it in too big a pot right away, you'll stunt it. You can't overfeed it, you can't over-borrow. Same as overfeeding your plants: you need to take time, have patience, and actually look at the data. That was a whole panel discussion at Ignited in Chicago this year — that M&A this year and next is going to be fast and furious. A friend of mine said the pitch right now for ERP is: if you want any of the companies out there talking M&A to come examine you, you'd better be able to show clean books, clean processes, a full list of liabilities, a full list of assets with depreciation, and some track record of how the business has performed. Otherwise, why would they buy you? What is there to buy — a shiny spaceship somebody paid thirty-two million dollars for seven years ago that's now worth ten cents on the dollar?

Host: Most of these companies are using Google Sheets well outside of what they're actually good for — and that's what shocks me most. Instead of going from Google Sheets to functioning tools built for the specific use case, they skip straight to vibe coding, and now they've dug themselves another hole, because it's just not going to work.

Chris Guthrie: If a company is really going to go from Google Sheets straight to vibe coding — watch out. You're going to fail. That's a path to failure. Please don't do that. You'll fail.

Host: I think this is the point where the industry is starting to separate — the big players with the means are figuring out what they do well and don't do well, and offloading the parts they don't do well as the industry changes. Then you've got other players doing fine in maybe one market, thinking about how to grow, and they land on cutting costs and building tools internally. I can't shake these companies enough to think hard about what they're actually investing in — the approach needs to change. What's the goal, and how do we get there? It doesn't have to be about cutting cost, it can be about optimizing the process — which means understanding exactly where your costs go, what drives them, and where you can actually save.

Chris Guthrie: Right, and I don't think you're going to vibe code something that gives you a true, reliable standard cost. Take Josh D.'s Motorbreath right here — do these guys know precisely what went into that flower, the cost of the jar, the label, the wait time? Seed-to-sale doesn't do that. By the time you finish your Saturday vibe coding session, you might think you've accounted for all of it, but you're pushing that down the hill — and what if it doesn't work? If you're a CFO: take your annual salary, divide it by the days you work and the hours you work. That whole time, you just spent probably seven thousand dollars of company time vibe coding an ERP that doesn't work — and now you're going to spend another seven thousand to go back and fix it. Just counting the people's time, you can calculate exactly what your vibe coding expedition cost. Keep track of it.

Host: Do you think this is part of the origin of the problem — companies ending up with patchwork software that never connected well, got disappointed, and landed on "well, I could switch, or I could just build it myself"?

Chris Guthrie: Change management is the number one reason ERP projects don't get adopted, and probably why they end up failing. I was in a year-and-a-half-long sales cycle with a top-five company in the country. The overall conclusion at the end was: this is what we need to do, but we're in fourteen or sixteen states, multiple facilities per state, a lot of it from acquisitions — different cultures, different processes, different data structures. The effort to align hundreds of people, first to figure out what they're actually doing, then to define a new company-wide national process, deploy it, and train on it, was too much. Once you get into the nitty-gritty of who touches what, when, and all the interdependencies across the people in an organization, it's genuinely complex — and that complexity, and the fear that you don't have the bandwidth to organize your business, is what keeps people from doing it.

Host: But the house of cards eventually falls. It's okay to ignore it for a while, but at some point you have to address the elephant you shoved in the room and closed the door on — "I'm never going back in there, I don't care how many times you ask me to look, I won't turn around." Eventually you have to deal with it, and I get it, now's never a good time.

Chris Guthrie: But it's still in there.

Host: This is the kind of conversation where, as the industry matures, if you can't process it, you get left behind. There's never a right time — there's always something going on, always a problem — but this needs to become the kind of priority that happened yesterday. That's the fear I have for companies avoiding it, because change is hard. But if not now, then when?

Chris Guthrie: The best time to plant a tree was twenty years ago. The next best time is today. Everybody's just been trying to survive the past two years — nobody was thinking about their five-, ten-, fifteen-year plan in 2023. Everything was in the toilet, nothing but broken dreams.

Host: Sure, but that's the frustration for me — the same teams thinking about vibe coding to cut costs could be using those same resources to get everyone onto the same foundation, so the same data tracked in Ohio and in Virginia is actually the same data.

Chris Guthrie: Yeah. People know what they need, but maybe it's some kind of Stockholm syndrome from being in the cannabis industry too long — building your business out on another shaky branch without even knowing where it leads. Maybe that just seems like the natural way to do it.

Host: So how do you get them to change? When you have that conversation and they know it's a massive uphill battle with no denying it, and it's going to take forever — they can ignore it, or they can get started. How do you help them see the benefit of changing in this environment?

Chris Guthrie: First thing I always do is make sure I understand what they're actually asking for. I've had discovery calls where someone opens with "I need some software to fix my business, man," and I reflexively say, "I don't sell that." What I will do is help you measure your business. Going through an ERP exercise can help you organize the business and surface what you don't know about it. If you want to shore things up, going through an ERP exercise is the most comprehensive business analysis, process-improvement, and measurement exercise there is — because everything has to go into the system correctly for it to function. I'll show them everything they want to see, walk through what the project looks like, and often they say, "I can't afford that." My next question is always: what happens if you do nothing? If this, then this; if this, then this. If you do ERP, you'll know these things. If you don't, what happens? Sometimes they say, "we'll figure it out," and I know they're headed out on the Oregon Trail and they're going to die of dysentery — good luck. Sometimes there's a version of "you've given us a lot to think about, here's how we need to move forward," and there's hope. The only reliable way I've found to change people's minds is to let them try it their way, and hopefully six or eight months later I hear, "we tried this and it didn't work, we know what we need now, and it's ERP." If ERP is done correctly, the ROI is two years, minimum — just from not missing orders, ordering things on time, being able to predict what your business will look like, instead of looking at the descriptive, after-the-fact data of what happened today.

Host: Or the Google Sheet where they say, "look at all my numbers, isn't it beautiful."

Chris Guthrie: "Look how many colors I've got on my tabs, I spent three hours color coding this." Great — that's a twelve-hundred-dollar color scheme.

Host: I have a real problem with Google Sheets and their colors — it's very triggering for me. You look at it and it tells you absolutely nothing. It actually gives me anxiety. I ask what any of it means, and they say, "this number's good, this number's bad." How'd you get those numbers? "I don't know." Cool — well, that number seems good, glad we've got green and red, and we'll never actually know the difference, but we've got green and red.

Chris Guthrie: Definitely — and I know they spent real time considering those colors, making sure they used the right shade of orange for this and the right shade for that. That's brainpower, time, and money literally on fire.

Host: Are there any takeaways for people who are on the fence — doesn't have to be ERP-specific, but you've seen a lot of different software tools and teams in this space. Anything you want people to think about, especially given how quickly the world is changing?

Chris Guthrie: First — the last Dime episode with Hirsch, I listened to it twice, it blew my mind, he's insane, such a good conversation. One thing I keep thinking about: Schedule 3, and what happens if the Epstein files situation blows up and Trump has to decriminalize and legalize cannabis just to get people talking about something else — or not talking about it? If the FDA gets involved, there are laws, procedures, standards, and inspections that will instantly govern cannabis, similar to tobacco or vape — it'll be treated as cosmetic, as food. There is no Google spreadsheet in the world that's going to meet those standards.

Host: They really don't. The FDA measures things a specific way, and it's built on traceability and defensibility. Pointing them to a Google Sheet won't go well. You said "if" — I'd say more "when," and I think that's the better mindset for teams, because at least then they'll be prepared. If it's "if this happens, we're not prepared" — it'd be better for teams to be in front of the change instead of behind it, because right now it feels like we're always reactive.

Chris Guthrie: Yes — and staying reactive is the same as depending on descriptive data. I work with a lot of Canadians, so I'll use their phrase: you've got to skate to where the puck is going. The FDA is going to get involved, full stop. When I said "if," it's only because the process is so messy and haphazard — executive orders, like what we saw with the Supreme Court yesterday, don't just make something so by declaration. It'll take time to get clarification on what Schedule 3 actually means.

Host: Sure, but the benefit is that they govern by a set of rules that already exist. The unknowns don't have to be invented — they just have to be followed.

Chris Guthrie: Yes, already there. And companies need to stop telling themselves and their shareholders they don't know what's going to happen. You can predict — you'd better be able to report what's in that jar the same way Philip Morris reports what's in a pack of Marlboros, or Olay reports what's in a jar of cream, or Hostess reports what's in a cupcake. It better have a change log, it better be publicly hosted, it better follow GAAP accounting principles, and if you're cultivating, it better follow GACP — generally accepted cultivation practices. These rules already exist. The question is whether you're setting your business up for the next phase of the industry, because it's not about balls anymore. It's careful, thoughtful prediction based on your current data. That's how business works.

Host: What question do you wish more people asked you?

Chris Guthrie: What is the actual ROI of ERP? It depends on the size of the project — when I say two years, I'm talking about something like a five-hundred-thousand-dollar project.

Host: Is two years too long for some teams, or too fast? To me that's fast, but I can imagine some teams hearing "two years" and saying no way.

Chris Guthrie: The one phrase I never want to hear again is "one month in the cannabis industry is like a year in any other industry." Sure, that's a great line, but it's also an excuse to slow down. You've got to know where the ROI actually is. My bullseye goal is to save an organization an hour a day across ten people — not going back and forth, not walking down the hall, not harassing someone for their cultivation spreadsheet, not wandering the warehouse wondering where something is, not chasing whether the soil shipment came in. Ten hours across ten people a day — do the math. Take your accounting team, say you save them thirty minutes a day — two and a half hours a day across the working days, that's instant, measurable ROI. "Works" means more than a working prototype: it means data is reliably recorded, organized in structured tables, and actually flows correctly between departments (e.g., harvest data feeding drying-room and manufacturing records).

Vibe-coded tools built without a Git repository or real dev environment accumulate invisible tech debt — when something breaks weeks later, there's often no way to trace back to the change that caused it.

AI can't infer the downstream effects of a data or field change across a business; it only works from the context and data you explicitly give it, and that data has to be clean and well-structured to be useful.

Total cost of a vibe-coded internal tool includes far more than the initial build: cloud hosting, ongoing AI token consumption per query, and the labor cost of the hours spent building and then rebuilding it when it breaks.

faq.question: Why shouldn't cannabis companies build their own internal software with AI/vibe coding?
faq.answer: Because almost no mature industry vibe-codes its core operational systems, and doing so tends to create invisible tech debt, unreliable data structures, and tools that can't withstand real day-to-day use by production and cultivation teams.

faq.question: What does it actually mean for internal software to "work," beyond just running?
faq.answer: It means inventory and process data is consistently recorded, organized into structured tables, and correctly flows between departments and systems — not just that a prototype runs on the day it was built.

faq.question: What hidden costs come with a vibe-coded internal tool?
faq.answer: Cloud hosting costs, ongoing AI token usage every time the tool is queried, and the labor cost of the time spent building it — plus the cost of rebuilding it when it breaks, which it eventually does.

faq.question: Why is a vibe-coded ERP or CRM a red flag during M&A due diligence?
faq.answer: Acquirers evaluating a company's tech stack read homegrown, vibe-coded tools as a sign of weak processes, unreliable books, and poor decision-making infrastructure — the opposite of what they want to see before buying a business.

faq.question: Why is cannabis seed-to-sale software mostly descriptive rather than predictive?
faq.answer: Most cannabis software (built on Metrc or BioTrack "skins") was designed to record what already happened, not to forecast. Getting real predictive insight requires a trusted ERP foundation with a proper data schema, not just feeding raw historical records to an AI.

faq.question: What is the actual ROI timeline for implementing a proper ERP system?
faq.answer: For a project on the scale of roughly $500,000, ROI is typically around two years minimum — driven by measurable time savings (e.g., an hour a day across ten employees) plus better cost visibility and predictive planning.

faq.question: How should cannabis companies prepare for potential FDA involvement (e.g., under rescheduling)?
faq.answer: By adopting already-established standards now — GAAP accounting principles and GACP (generally accepted cultivation practices) — and building traceable, defensible record-keeping, since spreadsheets and ad hoc systems won't meet FDA-level compliance requirements.

faq.question: What is the biggest reason ERP implementations fail, according to Chris Guthrie?
faq.answer: Change management — the difficulty of aligning people, processes, and data structures across multiple facilities, states, and acquisitions — more than any shortcoming of the software itself.
